overview: The card does not treat “Proto-Scythian culture” as an ancient self-name or a securely bounded people. It spans 700 to 500 BCE, with a polygon from the lower Danube and north Black Sea region toward the Don. It includes Iasi, Chisinau, Odesa, Dnipro, Mariupol, and Donetsk in point tests, but excludes forest-steppe sites such as Nemyriv and Bilsk. It shares arcs with Cimerians, Thrace, and chernoles-culture. Human-remain research describes a non-homogeneous forest-steppe population and differences from sampled steppe groups. Its author warns that cremation leaves no crania for comparison, so the surviving series is not a population census and cannot identify all residents of the polygon. The card uses “Proto-Scythian” only for the atlas layer and dates comparisons. Its eight evidence bands organize reading; they are not asserted historical phases. The map feature appears only in the 700 BCE snapshot, and points repaint at both seams. When the feature vanishes at 500 BCE, that software change alone cannot establish migration, conquest, biological replacement, or population disappearance.

periods.title: The atlas layer opens, but no people begins
periods.summary: The exact id appears only in the 700 BCE snapshot. Tunnug 1, an early animal-style assemblage in Tuva, dates about 833 to 800 BCE and lies far east of the mapped polygon. That distant comparison cannot date a migration, ethnic birth, political foundation, or synchronized archaeological beginning inside this software boundary.

periods.title: Foreign records name a ruler, not the polygon
periods.summary: An Assyrian oracle query concerns a contemplated treaty and marriage with Bartatua, king of the Scythians. The query belongs to Esarhaddon’s reign, 680 to 669 BCE, which overlaps this editorial band but does not date the episode more narrowly. It cannot name every community, language, or assemblage inside the atlas shape.

periods.title: Sources describe distinct communities and settings
periods.summary: Forest-steppe research describes clustered settlements, production, and social complexity, while biological research finds heterogeneous communities associated with Scythian material. These are incomplete modern samples, not a census. This editorial band keeps different lifeways and material similarities visible without merging them into one ethnicity.

periods.title: Two separate finds illustrate attribution limits
periods.summary: Malynivtsi Barrow 4 combines inhumation and cremation and is dated from the last third of the seventh through first half of the sixth century BCE. Separately, the Met catalogs a circa seventh-to-sixth-century Eurasian bronze harness or bridle fitting as “Scythian (?)”. Neither establishes a connection or regional trend.

periods.title: One looted woman’s grave anchors local evidence
periods.summary: At Skorobir, Mound 1/2021 contained a woman in a timbered grave with pottery, beads, and gold rosette plaques. Excavators date it to the first quarter of the sixth century, note looting, and interpret her as local elite. This is mortuary evidence about one person, not a regional political system.

periods.title: A closely dated grave anchors one local sequence
periods.summary: Bilsk Barrow 1/2020 is dated about 580/570 to 560/550 BCE and held handmade pottery, horse bits, a spearhead, and a quiver. The excavator’s link to a westward campaign remains a hypothesis. One grave anchors chronology; it does not define everyone inside the map.

periods.title: Different diets and movements resist one stereotype
periods.summary: Isotope research at Ukrainian sites finds local mobility signals and varied diets, challenging a model of universally roaming warrior nomads. Selected burials span wider dates. They reveal diverse lifeways without mapping one population, state, or border onto the atlas shape.

periods.title: The atlas label closes at a software seam
periods.summary: By about 500 BCE, the Cambridge synthesis describes named Scythians as a major military power. The exact target disappears at the 500 BCE software seam and does not return at 400 BCE. This is an editorial endpoint, not evidence of extinction, conquest, or wholesale population replacement.

sections.title: Read the atlas label and geometry

items.text: “Proto-Scythian culture” is a modern atlas label; no reviewed source establishes it as an attested self-name. Genetic research finds temporally and geographically distinct Scythian-associated communities heterogeneous, and shared cultural elements do not establish one ethnicity. The card treats the feature as an archaeology layer whose exact intended identity and population remain unresolved.

The stored feature is one Polygon with one ring, sixty-one positions, and bounds from about 25.97 to 42.55 east and 44.58 to 50.02 north. Those coordinates describe software geometry. They do not measure residence, grazing circuits, language, descent, allegiance, or any synchronous political frontier.

Representative-point tests place Iasi, Chisinau, Tiraspol, Odesa, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mariupol, Donetsk, and Galati inside the shape. Nemyriv, Vinnytsia, Kyiv, Cherkasy, Bilsk, Crimea, Rostov, and Voronezh fall outside. Point membership reports geometry only; it is never an archaeological, historical, or ethnic identity test.

At 700 BCE the target shares direct TopoJSON arcs with several Cimerians features, Thrace, and chernoles-culture. Shared arcs expose how the atlas partitions its picture; they do not prove negotiated ancient borders. The same year still assigns nearby control points to different labels, warning against reading one seamless cultural block.

Between the 1000 and 700 BCE snapshots, many southern controls repaint from Cimerians to the target; northern controls repaint to chernoles-culture. At 500 BCE the target vanishes and most controls become unlabeled. These abrupt changes are atlas seams, not dated conquests, migrations, demographic collapse, or cultural extinction.

sections.title: Separate chronology, texts, and archaeological phases

items.text: Radiocarbon authors divide a broad Scythian epoch into a combined pre-Scythian and initial period, an Early Scythian period, and a classical period, while stating that beginnings differ across Eurasia. Their seventh-to-sixth-century Early Scythian phase overlaps the atlas range, but this scholarly periodization neither validates the exact polygon nor fixes one population’s lifespan.

North-eastern Azov burials classified as Chernogorivka, Novocherkassk, Cimmerian, or pre-Scythian precede sites the authors call Scythian-time. The vocabulary itself records interpretive choices. A sequence of changing assemblages is stronger evidence than a simple story in which one ethnic people instantly replaced another at 700 BCE.

The Esarhaddon-era marriage query names Bartatua as king of the Scythians and asks whether an Assyrian princess should be sent. This contemporary external source reveals diplomacy at a royal level. It supplies neither a native ethnonym spelling guide nor a boundary, census, constitution, or description of daily life.

A seventh-to-sixth-century bronze harness or bridle fitting in the Metropolitan Museum catalog is labeled “Scythian (?)”. Its question mark is valuable evidence practice: the date, medium, size, and broad Eurasian provenance are recorded more securely than cultural attribution. One unprovenanced object cannot anchor the atlas identity.

The earliest full animal-style assemblage discussed at Tunnug 1 dates about 833 to 800 BCE in Tuva, far east and earlier than this layer. It helps explain a trans-Eurasian artistic horizon and origin debate. It cannot be silently moved to the north Pontic polygon or equated with its inhabitants.

sections.title: Compare settlements, mobility, and political scale

items.text: Left-bank forest-steppe research reconstructs clusters of agricultural settlements with ashhills and a shared mound cemetery by the middle seventh century BCE. It also identifies mobile groups from burials along routes and likely wintering places. The model describes interaction between lifeways, not an entirely nomadic or culturally uniform landscape.

Isotope research across Iron Age Ukrainian sites finds many individuals with local mobility signals and varied diets, challenging the stock picture of universally roaming warrior nomads. The sample spans more than the atlas dates and several sites. Its result supports diversity, not a new claim that every person was sedentary.

The Cambridge synthesis describes sixth-century Scythian life as a core-periphery system with nomadism only one component, fortified centers, and large-scale trade. “Core” and “periphery” are analytical language. They do not identify a capital governing the atlas polygon or convert material exchange into state territory.

Bilsk’s earliest open settlements preceded its earthworks. Research proposes a wooden fence at the beginning of the third quarter of the sixth century BCE and stronger earthen ramparts later, while distinguishing phases and traditions. This changing built landscape should not be stretched into one permanently fortified political system for the atlas interval.

Urbanisation research tests fortification, production, exchange, ritual space, and settlement clustering rather than assuming that every large hillfort was a city. Bilsk population estimates and synchrony remain contested. Collective construction implies organization, yet the available evidence does not reveal a single ruler, bureaucracy, or border service for the atlas shape.

sections.title: Reconstruct food, animals, and water cautiously

items.text: Stable-isotope results from Ukrainian human remains show diets combining terrestrial plants and animal products, with variation among places and individuals. The study’s broad Scythian-era sample is direct bodily evidence but not a menu for 700 to 500 BCE alone. It rules out a single uniform diet more clearly than it specifies meals.

Dental-calculus proteomics identifies ruminant milk proteins in sampled Iron Age individuals from Ukraine. The method offers direct evidence that some people consumed dairy, while site selection, preservation, and small samples limit scale. It does not show that every household herded the same animals or processed milk identically.

A 2026 oral-health study examines thirty-six people from Bilsk, Medvin, and Mamai-Gora for caries, calculus, abscesses, tooth loss, and wear. Its evidence supports grain consumption and food processing in sampled communities across 700 to 200 BCE. It cannot isolate an atlas-wide diet for each fifty-year band.

Bilsk bead research distinguishes burials from settlement contexts that include dugouts, household pits, and ash hills. Greek ceramics and glassware document exchange with northern Black Sea centers, including a route associated with Olbia. This forest-steppe complex lies outside the atlas polygon, so it remains a regional comparison rather than a household template.

Settlement clusters followed the Vorskla and Psel river basins, while the atlas polygon crosses major rivers and the north Black Sea coast. Those river settings make water access a reasonable inference, but reviewed sources do not specify household wells, water ownership, treatment, or carrying routines across this layer.

sections.title: Examine houses, storage, fire, and seasonal movement

items.text: Bilsk excavations document dugouts, household pits, and ash-hill contexts from the late seventh century onward. These features show domestic and depositional activity in one large forest-steppe complex outside the atlas polygon. They cannot supply a standard house for earlier decades, mobile camps, or every community inside the mapped shape.

The settlement-system study links mobile burials to travel routes, frequent stops, and probable wintering, while farmers occupied clustered settlements. “Wintering” is the author’s reconstruction from site patterning. It supports seasonal movement as one lifeway but does not provide wagon counts, tent plans, camp size, or universal annual routes.

British Museum interpretation describes wagons used as shelters and horses central to movement, drawing on texts and archaeology from the wider Scythian world. These are useful comparative technologies. Their wide temporal and geographic frame means they cannot be assigned automatically to every north Pontic household between 700 and 500 BCE.

The first-quarter sixth-century woman’s grave at Skorobir had a rectangular pit, wooden-board floor, log supports, and a timber ceiling with pottery placed above. This is carefully recorded mortuary architecture, not an ordinary dwelling. Construction knowledge is visible, while domestic house form must come from settlement archaeology.

Early fortification research distinguishes open settlements, light fences, and later ramparts with wooden walls and moats. Such changes required timber, earth, labor, and planning. They are achievements of particular communities over time, and the proposed stages should not be collapsed into an exact 700 BCE construction event across the atlas.

sections.title: See families, women, children, and social difference

items.text: A study of 197 early Scythian-period burial complexes sorts graves into wealth classes, then warns that biological sex was rarely established and often inferred from objects. Jewelry also appears with males and weapons with females. Mortuary categories reveal inequality imperfectly; they are not a transparent family tree or household census.

The Skorobir woman buried in the first quarter of the sixth century received glass and rock-crystal beads plus gold rosette plaques. Excavators interpret her as local elite. Her grave shows that a woman could receive costly commemoration, but looting, selection, and mortuary display prevent a universal claim about women’s daily status.

Armed-women graves span the second half of the seventh century to the second or even first century BCE. The earliest graves date from the late seventh into early sixth century, while the main concentration is fourth-century. Weapons in graves do not prove all women fought or gender rules were uniform.

The Malynivtsi barrow combined inhumation and cremation, scattered remains, beads, pins, earrings, and many vessels. Researchers date it from the last third of the seventh through first half of the sixth century and associate it with ordinary local people. Burial community is visible; exact kin relationships are not.

Children certainly lived in these communities, yet the reviewed early-period sources do not provide a secure child household, school, age-grade curriculum, or parent-child pair tied to the exact atlas layer. Adult graves and settlement plans cannot fill that absence. The card leaves childhood structure unresolved rather than importing later ethnography.

sections.title: Trace learning, craft, technology, and exchange

items.text: Spindle whorls, loom evidence, and ceramic impressions support spinning and weaving in the left-bank forest-steppe from the seventh century onward. These technologies required practiced sequences, so skills were learned, but archaeology does not identify the learner’s age, teacher, lesson format, or whether knowledge passed only within families.

Forest-steppe production evidence includes stone-mold casting, lost-wax casting, wire drawing, plating, embossing, blacksmith workshops, and craft districts. Such coordinated work demonstrates specialist knowledge and transmission. The source does not let us reconstruct apprenticeships, name individual makers, or assign every workshop to people called Proto-Scythians.

A wrought copper cauldron near Bilsk was studied by morphology and X-ray fluorescence, then linked cautiously to central Caucasian production and Urartian influence. It may have moved with mobile groups. The object demonstrates technical and intercultural connections, while the authors’ “could have” wording must remain a hypothesis, not a migration fact.

First-half sixth-century quiver sets occur with Miletian, Klazomenian, and Teian transport or painted amphorae from sites spanning Kuban to the Dnieper forest-steppe. These paired finds refine chronology and show long-distance connections. They do not tell whether exchange was direct, peaceful, coerced, or controlled by one political center.

In wider Archaic and Classical named-Scythian evidence, Greek-facing exchange involved wine, tableware, expensive arms, interpreters, and goldsmiths, but long contact did not ensure mutual understanding. Encyclopaedia Iranica says Scythian lacks authentic continuous texts; evidence is indirect and chiefly names recorded by neighbors. No original-script sample, transliteration, and translation can securely represent this imported atlas layer.

sections.title: Discuss health, care, and medicine without invention

items.text: Teeth from thirty-six people show caries, calculus, abscesses, tooth loss, and wear, giving direct but uneven evidence of oral health and food processing. The study spans 700 to 200 BCE, so individual cases cannot automatically date to this layer. Pathology records lived conditions, not named diagnoses or treatments.

Isotope and mobility research samples human remains rather than elite objects, helping recover diet and movement at several Ukrainian sites. Even so, burial selection and preservation shape the dataset. The evidence does not reveal who nursed the ill, set bones, assisted births, or distributed food during sickness in each community.

Cocklebur appears in only three Scythian-period Ukrainian finds, including one random Bilsk find and two impressions in clay. The archaeobotanist says isolated evidence cannot establish use. A possible medicinal role comes from much later evidence, so it must not be presented as Early Scythian pharmacy or a treatment recipe.

Burial construction, objects, and repeated commemoration show that communities invested labor and materials in caring for the dead. They do not directly describe care for living bodies. British Museum comparisons span the wider Scythian world, so preserved mummies or distant practices cannot be transplanted into ordinary north Pontic life.

No reviewed source securely identifies a hospital, clinic, named healer, birth attendant, surgical manual, or pharmacopoeia for the exact 700 to 500 BCE atlas layer. That is a bounded documentary and archaeological gap. It does not mean people lacked care, remedies, expertise, or social obligations toward illness and injury.

sections.title: Handle waste, sanitation, and toilets as evidence gaps

items.text: Bilsk has excavated ash-hill, dugout, and household-pit contexts. These deposits record accumulated material, yet none automatically means toilet, sewer, or household rubbish bin. Feature function depends on context, contents, formation history, and excavation, not a modern sanitation label supplied for convenience.

A comparative study of forty-nine features at eleven mostly medieval British sites defines cesspits through converging insects, plant remains, artifacts, architecture, and context. It supplies a method, not local evidence. Therefore an unlabeled pit or ashhill in a Scythian-period settlement cannot be called a latrine without comparable direct indicators.

The settlement-system source discusses farmers, mobile groups, ashhills, routes, wintering, and cemeteries, but does not identify a toilet, privy, cesspit, drain, sewer, or fecal deposit for its seventh-to-sixth-century sites. This is a narrow source gap, not proof that people failed to manage human waste.

The Bilsk article names dugouts, household pits, ash hills, Greek ceramics, and exchange, without assigning any feature a sanitation function. No reviewed publication in this packet demonstrates piped water, standardized latrines, or a municipal sewer for this period and region. This is a bounded source finding, not proof that waste went unmanaged.

The Bilsk defensive-architecture study distinguishes settlement fences, wooden walls, ramparts, and moat construction, but does not identify any as a drain, sewer, toilet, or clean-water work. That bounded report leaves sanitation unresolved and prevents repurposing a defensive feature as evidence of waste disposal or water treatment.

Spindle whorls, loom evidence, ceramic impressions, and early animal-style objects show practiced design and material knowledge in different regions and periods. Similar forms and techniques could travel widely, but circulation does not identify one inventor or ethnicity. Achievement belongs to many makers and communities, not an undemonstrated Proto-Scythian nation.

The carefully built Skorobir grave used boards, logs, a passage, pottery, beads, and gold plaques to commemorate one woman. Its survival despite ancient looting reveals planning and skilled work. Calling her local elite is an archaeological interpretation; her name, language, kin group, and opinion remain unknown.

Bilsk’s settlements, production zones, fortification stages, and trade connections show substantial collective capacity. Scholars still debate whether such centers were urban and how many people occupied them simultaneously. The achievement is visible without declaring Bilsk capital of the atlas polygon or equating its residents with one homogeneous people.

Recent genetic research finds heterogeneity among geographically and temporally distinct Scythian-associated communities. Genomes do not speak ethnic self-identification, but they reinforce a crucial limit: shared objects and burial customs cannot establish one biological population, timeless nation, pure ancestry, common language, or single political allegiance.

After 500 BCE the exact imported label remains absent, while later Scythian-associated samples still represent geographically and temporally distinct communities. No successor id receives this polygon. The atlas seam therefore cannot demonstrate conquest, extinction, biological replacement, or a single population continuing unchanged; it marks a change in mapped classification.

ending.text: The exact proto-scythian-culture feature disappears at the 500 BCE atlas seam and remains absent at 400 BCE. No reviewed source establishes a people using that self-name, dissolving a government, suffering extinction, or transferring a bounded state to a successor. Radiocarbon authors instead divide a broad Scythian epoch into analytical periods and warn that beginnings differ across Eurasia. Their sequence does not make 500 BCE a simultaneous migration, biological replacement, or end of occupation everywhere inside the polygon. Because the imported layer is an archaeological-style umbrella rather than a demonstrated polity, its ending is best described as a classification transition. No successor id inherits this polygon. Later atlas silence cannot prove that people, skills, or networks disappeared; it records a change in mapping categories, while historical and archaeological evidence must be dated independently. The label ends; people living across these varied regions did not thereby vanish.
